newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIUM'S DI RUPO: Sex and the single currency.
newsitem.headline: BELGIUM'S DI RUPO: Sex and the single currency.

text.p: The Belgian government stepped back from the political -- and arguably economic -- precipice by clearing Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo of child sex charges, but in the process it has opened a Pandora's box.

Three weeks of debate ending in three days and nights of bitter argument may have cleared Di Rupo of the allegations he had sex with boys under the legal age of consent of 16 years, but it also exposed rifts in the coalition government.
Di Rupo, an acknowledged homosexual, had always denied the allegation and his fellow Socialist Party members supported him.
The Christian Democratic parties in Belgium's centre-left coalition government were more circumspect, although Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene had declared his faith in his deputy.

Political sources said that when the acrimonious debate in a parliamentary commission reached its final stages early on Thursday, Di Rupo's fellow francophone socialists had pulled out all the stops -- including threatening to quit the coalition.
It was, as one parliamentary source put it, a game of poker with extremely high stakes.
Neither the francophone nor the Flemish Socialist Parties want an election before the due date of 1999.

With deep public suspicion of the political classes and a mood in the country reminiscent of the hysterical denunciations of the McCarthy era in the United States in the 1950s, both corruption-tainted parties fear a thrashing at the ballot box.

An election now, or even a change in government partners for Dehaene's Flemish and francophone Christian Democrats, could also derail efforts to get the national finances in shape for joining the European Union's single currency in 1999.
Dehaene, a master of the backroom political compromise, is determined to the point of having tunnel vision that Belgium must be in the first group to join the single currency.

His government has pushed through special powers to allow it to deal with the country's massive public debts and its deficit -- which were allowed to run rampant during the 1980s when the francophone and Flemish Liberals last held power.
Slashing the debts and the deficit are key elements in the bid to join the single currency club.

Calling an election now would divert attention from this crucial task for at best weeks and, given the complicated nature of coalition-forming in Belgium, possibly months at a time when every day counts.

Changing the makeup of the coalition without an election would also hold huge risks given that any new team would doubtless involve the Liberals. These have a poor financial track record in government and are distrusted by those key financial policy police -- the money markets.
The Liberals, who took the lead in calling for Di Rupo's resignation, on Thursday promptly accused the government of a stitch-up.
"Justice has been turned into a saleable commodity," Louis Michel, leader of the Francophone Liberals said.
The general public seems to agree. A poll in the Derniere Heure newspaper on Friday showed that 56.9 percent of people believed the decision on Di Rupo had been purely political.

But in reluctantly agreeing to clear the number two in the government, the parliamentary commission also decided to change the way the system works -- a move that could still produce some serious shocks in coming months.

The commission agreed a draft law short-circuiting the cumbersome parliamentary procedure and allowing the Cour de Cassation, Belgium's highest court, to investigate allegations against government ministers without having to ask parliament.

However, the new law -- which must still be accepted by parliament -- also means that the court, the only body allowed to judge ministers, can investigate any further allegations that emerge about Di Rupo or any other minister for that matter.
